Report Card: Harties Hyacinth

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Where is the Hyacinth now? Has anything been done since the story's in February and June? We go and find out how the Department has dealt with the situation.

Unique Selling Point:
We will speak to Ian Gun from Joy's story - on how nothing has changed and the tourism industry is now starting, yet nothing has changed. They are asking for the area to be sprayed, like what happened at Roodeplaatz dam. This is drastic, but might be the only way of curbing the growth.
Dr. Frikkie Botha from the June story is on the rehabilitation committee - he says that they are a private organization and the government has left it to them after many engagements. He says they are planning on massive harvesting, but it's getting worse, because now it's summer and the Hyacinth is starting to grow again - it's already changed in colour from brown to bright green.
The department of water affairs was on 50/50 saying they have put out tenders, but those were supposed to start in September, but nothing has started yet.

Extra Budget Items:
We need a drone to show the hyacinth

Script:


This looks like a golf course but it’s actually an aerial view of the Hartbeespoort Dam in January this year. Chairman of their tourism association, Iain Gunn, said government had failed the community.
Iain: “There is a plan on paper – it will go down to another 20 – 30 meetings by that time this whole beautiful dam we see behind us will be one big green patch of beautiful lawn.”
This aquatic weed doubles every 11-18 days feeding off nutrient washed down from rivers upstream. When we went back in April, at the beginning of winter when the hyacinth should be dormant, it covered 30% of the dam. The Department of Water and Sanitation’s Sputnik Ratau said they were monitoring the situation.
Sputnik: “Monitoring is meant to assist that when that failure happens in order to be able to correct that failure.”
This week we returned to the Dam to find out whether the department had corrected its failures. Sadly, these aerials show the green suffocating mass is thriving. Microbiologist Dr. Frikkie Botha, who is chairman on the dam’s steering or rehabilitation committee has been scientifically tracking the growth of the hyacinth.
Dr. Botha: “It is still in the order of 30% but take into account that we removed 60 thousand tonnes.”
He says the rains washed a lot of the nutrient into the river feeding the rapid-growing plant, added to that, is the fact that it’s no longer dormant and has turned bright green.
Dr. Botha: “If we do nothing, and we accept this growth rate, then I’ve made a calculation that in April next year we will be 100% covered on the dam.”
Iain Gunn says it’s now high season for tourists, but water and sanitation only met with residents in late September.
Gunn: “They’ve implemented 3 contracts now to start removing the hyacinth. It’s going to grow faster than what they can remove. The department of water and sanitation need funding, naturally that authorisation comes from above, so who authorises that funding?”
Gunn says the government’s only option now may be to spray the hyacinth with herbicide.
Gunn: “There is new chemicals that have been produced. People from department of water and sanitation had very positive reports.”
Botha: “We will fight the introduction of any herbicide, because of the detrimental effects it may have on the whole ecological system.”
The department did not grant an on-camera interview this time, and after missing several deadlines to answer our written questions has failed to respond at all. Dr. Botha says the department has given few resources, other than some cabling to assist in containing the hyacinth, but they have issued a license to harvest the plant and have promulgated a resource management plan to form an interim dam committee. However, no funds have been contributed and the community, through its new website, has raised R580,000. For their community engagement the Department of Water and Sanitation receive a D.
Botha: “We have been trying to get action out of them without any results so my estimate of their performance is a 2 or a 3.”
So for their lack of action a double F.
Gunn: “Well communications directly with the department is a minus 1. Communication with internal elements 10 out of 10. I think the planning I would be a zero, because this is going for years.”
For their poor Communication and Planning also a double F.
Gunn: “The people who live here are doing something. And even if that something is only taking one teaspoon out a day, its one teaspoon more than what government has assisted us with.”
The Department of Water and Sanitation for their failing to respond to our questions and for not dealing with the looming hyacinth disaster has failed dismally.
